Educación y formación 10 casos de uso · 8 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve5 tendencias
  • Los jóvenes ya usan la IA para estudiar: según datos de Eurostat citados por la Comisión Europea, 4 de cada 10 residentes de la UE de 16 a 24 años usaron IA generativa en su educación formal en 2025. Un centro que no la ordena la tiene igualmente en el aula.f3
  • Mejor tarea no es mejor aprendizaje: la Comisión Europea recoge que los alumnos aprenden más cuando la IA apoya su propio pensamiento, que las herramientas educativas rinden en general más que las de uso general y que depender de la IA puede debilitar el pensamiento crítico.f3
  • El docente sigue siendo el centro: la UNESCO propone un enfoque centrado en la persona, con uso ético, seguro, equitativo y significativo, y un límite de edad para las conversaciones independientes con IA generativa. La guía española del INTEF (versión 2.0, septiembre de 2026) recomienda priorizar herramientas puestas a disposición o autorizadas por las administraciones educativas.f1f5
  • Falta formación: solo el 29,7 % de los docentes de la UE encuestados en TALIS 2024 había recibido formación profesional sobre IA para enseñar y aprender. Las directrices éticas de la Comisión Europea ayudan a docentes con poca experiencia digital.f3f2
  • Riesgo específico de la educación: hay menores, y los datos de los alumnos exigen protección reforzada. Los sistemas de IA que evalúan resultados del aprendizaje, deciden el acceso o la admisión o vigilan las pruebas son de alto riesgo en el Reglamento de IA, y los que infieren emociones del alumnado son una práctica prohibida en educación. La AEPD y otras autoridades recuerdan que usar una plataforma educativa no es voluntario para alumnos y familias, y piden evaluación de impacto, contrato de encargado y protección de datos por defecto.f7f8f6f4f5
Cifras4 cifras con fuente

  • 29,7 % · Docentes de la UE encuestados en TALIS 2024 que habían recibido formación profesional sobre IA para enseñar y aprenderf3
  • 10 · Principios básicos del decálogo de las autoridades de protección de datos para contratar y usar plataformas educativas (23-03-2026)f4

Aviso temprano de riesgo de abandono por asistencia y entregasML predictivo07 · DecisiónOptimizar

Avisa al tutor cuando faltan clases o entregas seguidas, con datos que el centro ya tiene; sin vigilar al alumno ni medir emociones, y la acción la decide una persona.f5f6f7

Función
Tutoría
Palanca de valor
Riesgo y cumplimiento
Tecnología y técnicas habituales
ML predictivo. Modelos que aprenden de datos históricos con resultado conocido. Lo más usado con datos en tablas: árboles potenciados por gradiente (XGBoost, LightGBM), bosques aleatorios y regresión logística como línea base explicable. Para anomalías: bosques de aislamiento o autocodificadores. Para series en el tiempo: modelos estadísticos o redes recurrentes. Pida siempre la comparación con una línea base sencilla.

Marketing, publicidad y comunicación 12 casos de uso · 11 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve5 tendencias
  • La IA ya es herramienta de trabajo en publicidad: según IAB Europe, el 85 % de las empresas de la encuesta (anunciantes, agencias, tecnología publicitaria y medios) usa herramientas de IA para marketing, y el 60 % de las empresas de tecnología publicitaria y el 48 % de las agencias dicen haber mejorado sus indicadores. La agencia pequeña que no la use compite en desventaja.f1
  • Los anunciantes piden reglas claras: de 27 grandes marcas, el 78 % usa contenido generado o mejorado con IA de cara al consumidor, el 67 % tiene normas internas y ocho de cada diez piden una guía global; la mayoría cree que una voz de IA que pueda confundirse con una persona debe indicarse. El cliente pedirá a la agencia que sepa decir qué es IA y qué no.f4
  • La propiedad intelectual es el miedo principal: el 77 % de las marcas de un estudio de la WFA destaca los riesgos de propiedad intelectual y derechos de autor de la IA generativa. La oficina de propiedad intelectual de la UE describe el choque entre el uso de obras para entrenar modelos, la reserva de derechos de los autores (opt-out) y el derecho a licenciar; la oficina de derechos de autor de Estados Unidos concluye que, con la tecnología actual, las instrucciones escritas por sí solas no dan control suficiente para ser autor y que lo creado solo por IA no se protege.f5f2f3
  • La autorregulación ya se mueve: el código de conducta sobre publicidad con influencers de AUTOCONTROL, la aea e IAB Spain entró en vigor el 1 de octubre de 2025 con previsiones específicas sobre contenidos generados con IA. Quien produce piezas para marcas debe conocerlo y aplicarlo.f6
  • Riesgo específico del sector: el Reglamento de IA (art. 50) obliga a marcar el contenido sintético y las ultrafalsificaciones, y la Comisión ha publicado un código de buenas prácticas sobre marcado y etiquetado y unas directrices del art. 50. Además, el RGPD y la LOPDGDD limitan la segmentación con datos personales, y lo generado puede copiar obras ajenas. Una persona revisa cada pieza antes de publicarla, y el contrato con el cliente dice quién responde de qué.f8f10f9f11f7
Cifras8 cifras con fuente
  • 85 % · Empresas de publicidad digital europeas que usan herramientas de IA para marketing (encuesta de cerca de 100 empresas)f1
  • 68 % / 43 % · Empresas con normas internas de IA en general / específicas para marketing y publicidadf1
  • 78 % · Marcas globales que usan contenido generado o mejorado con IA de cara al consumidorf4
  • 67 % · Marcas globales con normas internas de IAf4
  • 96 % · Marcas que dicen que una voz de IA que el público podría tomar por humana debe indicarsef4
  • 77 % · Marcas que declaran la propiedad intelectual y los derechos de autor como su mayor preocupación con la IA generativaf5
  • 40 % · Marcas que adoptan IA generativa y la usan en comunicaciones de marketing de cara al usuariof5
  • más de 17 millones · Empleos de los sectores intensivos en derechos de autor en la UEf2

Tecnología y técnicas habituales
ML predictivo. Modelos que aprenden de datos históricos con resultado conocido. Oficios, reformas y servicios a domicilio 9 casos de uso · 9 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve5 tendencias
  • El oficio es, sobre todo, un negocio de una persona. En septiembre de 2026 había 3.505.556 autónomos afiliados a la Seguridad Social; el 85,9 % no tiene asalariados y el 12,0 % trabaja en construcción. Para un autónomo, la IA útil es la que le ahorra horas de papeleo y de llamadas, no la que exige montar un sistema.f1
  • La IA ya llega a las empresas más pequeñas: usa IA el 17 % de las pequeñas empresas de la UE (10 a 49 empleados) y el 21,36 % de las españolas de menos de 10 empleados. Lo más habitual es empezar por texto: presupuestos, mensajes a clientes y partes de trabajo.f6f7
  • El papeleo técnico es obligatorio y tiene responsable. El Reglamento electrotécnico de baja tensión exige que la empresa instaladora emita el certificado de instalación y lo deposite ante la Comunidad Autónoma. El Reglamento de instalaciones térmicas exige un registro de las operaciones de mantenimiento y un certificado anual cuando hay contrato obligatorio. La IA prepara el borrador; firma el profesional habilitado.f2f3
  • Una reforma deja responsabilidades largas. La Ley de Ordenación de la Edificación fija responsabilidad por daños de diez años (estructura), tres años (habitabilidad) y un año (acabados). Guardar con orden fotos, partes y materiales de cada obra es la mejor defensa ante una reclamación.f4
  • Riesgo específico del oficio: se trabaja en casas de clientes, con sus fotos, direcciones y llaves, y a veces con personal que se desplaza. Hace falta base legal, tratar solo los datos necesarios y no guardar fotos del interior de una vivienda más tiempo del necesario (RGPD). Seguir la ruta de un vehículo no es vigilar a una persona: los sistemas de gestión de trabajadores con IA son un uso delicado, y el Reglamento de IA los trata con especial cuidado.f5f9f8
Cifras8 cifras con fuente
  • 3.505.556 · Autónomos afiliados a la Seguridad Social (septiembre de 2026)f1
  • 12,0 % · Autónomos que trabajan en el sector de la construcción (septiembre de 2026)f1
  • 85,9 % · Autónomos que no tienen ningún asalariado (septiembre de 2026)f1
  • 21,36 % · Empresas españolas con menos de 10 empleados que usaron IA (primer trimestre de 2026)f7
  • 17 % · Empresas pequeñas (10-49) de la UE que usan IA, 2025f6
  • 10 / 3 / 1 · Años de garantía por daños estructurales, de habitabilidad y de acabados en la edificaciónf4
  • 5 años · Años mínimos que se conserva el registro de operaciones de mantenimiento de una instalación térmicaf3
  • 6 % / 19 % · Organizaciones de la UE con 5 a 9 empleados que usan sistemas para vigilar el rendimiento de los trabajadores, frente a las de 250 o másf5

Talleres e industria pequeña 12 casos de uso · 10 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve5 tendencias
  • El Reglamento de Datos ya se aplica: la Comisión Europea dice que será aplicable desde el 12 de septiembre de 2025 y que quien usa un producto conectado, como un coche o una máquina industrial, tiene derecho a acceder a los datos que genera y a compartirlos con terceros, entre ellos quien lo repara. Para un taller, más datos del vehículo y de la máquina a su alcance.f1
  • La Comisión ha publicado orientaciones sobre datos de vehículos para acompañar el Reglamento de Datos, que cubren también a los prestadores de servicios del mercado de posventa, y un reglamento delegado de 23 de marzo de 2026 impide que un fabricante condicione el acceso de los agentes independientes a la información de diagnóstico y reparación a requisitos distintos de los del reglamento de homologación, por ejemplo por razones de ciberseguridad.f2f3
  • El nuevo Reglamento de máquinas será de plena aplicación desde el 20 de enero de 2027, según el Instituto Nacional de Seguridad y Salud en el Trabajo, y incluye entre sus categorías de mayor riesgo los componentes de seguridad con comportamiento autoevolutivo que usan aprendizaje automático. Quien fabrica o modifica máquinas, aunque sea pequeño, debe seguirlo de cerca.f4f9
  • La automatización crece en los lugares de trabajo y trae oportunidades y riesgos nuevos para la seguridad y la salud, según la Agencia Europea para la Seguridad y la Salud en el Trabajo (EU-OSHA), que propone evaluarlos tarea por tarea.f5
  • Riesgo específico de los talleres y los fabricantes pequeños: una herramienta de IA que toque una máquina o su función de seguridad cambia el análisis de riesgos de la máquina (Reglamento de máquinas), las fotos de clientes y vehículos pueden contener matrículas y personas (RGPD) y un sistema de IA que sea componente de seguridad de un producto regulado puede ser de alto riesgo (Reglamento de IA). La persona responsable revisa siempre el diagnóstico, el presupuesto y la decisión de seguridad.f9f10f8
Cifras3 cifras con fuente
  • 12-09-2025 · Fecha desde la que es aplicable el Reglamento de Datos (acceso a los datos de productos conectados)f1
  • 23-03-2026 · Fecha del reglamento delegado sobre acceso normalizado a la información de diagnóstico a bordo y de reparación de vehículosf3
  • 20-01-2027 · Fecha de plena aplicación del Reglamento (UE) 2023/1230 de máquinasf4

Mantenimiento predictivo de pocas máquinas con sensores baratosML predictivo04 · OperacionesOptimizar

Sensores de vibración, temperatura o consumo en las máquinas clave avisan de un desgaste anormal antes de la parada; el responsable decide cuándo intervenir.f1f9

Función
Mantenimiento
Palanca de valor
Eficiencia
Tecnología y técnicas habituales
ML predictivo. Modelos que aprenden de datos históricos con resultado conocido. Lo más usado con datos en tablas: árboles potenciados por gradiente (XGBoost, LightGBM), bosques aleatorios y regresión logística como línea base explicable. Para anomalías: bosques de aislamiento o autocodificadores. Para series en el tiempo: modelos estadísticos o redes recurrentes. Pida siempre la comparación con una línea base sencilla.

Transporte pequeño y autónomos del transporte 10 casos de uso · 10 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve4 tendencias
  • El documento de transporte se vuelve digital en la Unión Europea: la Comisión Europea dice que el Reglamento eFTI quiere sustituir el papel por datos electrónicos en todos los modos de transporte, que se aplicará en su totalidad el 9 de julio de 2027 y que las autoridades de los Estados miembros deberán aceptar la información compartida por plataformas certificadas.f1
  • En España, el documento de control administrativo del transporte público de mercancías por carretera debe ser digital a los diez meses de la entrada en vigor de la Ley 9/2025, de 3 de diciembre, y la hoja de ruta del transporte de personas, también. Una resolución de 5 de junio de 2026 fija cómo deben ser los programas que lo gestionan. Afecta a los transportes interiores y al cabotaje, no a los internacionales.f3
  • El tacógrafo inteligente de segunda versión llega también a las furgonetas: la Comisión Europea indica que los vehículos comerciales ligeros de más de 2,5 toneladas en transporte internacional deben llevarlo desde el 1 de julio de 2026. Más datos de conducción y descanso, y más control sobre ellos.f2
  • Riesgo específico del transporte: seguir al conductor con GPS, tacógrafo o cámaras es tratar datos de trabajadores. La Agencia Española de Protección de Datos recuerda que la geolocalización de vehículos de la empresa se apoya en el contrato de trabajo y no en el consentimiento, que hay que informar al conductor, que se aplica la minimización y que una cámara en cabina con grabación de vídeo y sonido para vigilar la conducción no prevalece sobre su derecho a la protección de datos. Cualquier IA que vigile fatiga o conducción necesita análisis de impacto, información previa y revisión humana; los sistemas de IA para gestionar personas pueden ser de alto riesgo, y quien trabaja para plataformas tiene protección propia.f4f7f10f8f9
Cifras5 cifras con fuente
  • 9-07-2027 · Fecha de plena aplicación del Reglamento eFTI (documentos de transporte electrónicos aceptados por las autoridades)f1
  • 1.000 millones de euros · Ahorro anual previsto por la Comisión Europea en costes operativos y administrativos del transporte y la logística de la UE con eFTIf1
  • 1-07-2026 · Fecha desde la que los vehículos comerciales ligeros de más de 2,5 toneladas en transporte internacional deben llevar tacógrafo inteligente de segunda versiónf2
  • 18-08-2025 · Fecha límite para sustituir un tacógrafo inteligente de primera versión en transporte internacionalf2
  • 10 meses · Plazo desde la entrada en vigor de la Ley 9/2025 para que el documento de control del transporte de mercancías por carretera sea digitalf3

Función
Mantenimiento
Palanca de valor
Riesgo y cumplimiento
Tecnología y técnicas habituales
ML predictivo. Modelos que aprenden de datos históricos con resultado conocido. Lo más usado con datos en tablas: árboles potenciados por gradiente (XGBoost, LightGBM), bosques aleatorios y regresión logística como línea base explicable. Para anomalías: bosques de aislamiento o autocodificadores. Para series en el tiempo: modelos estadísticos o redes recurrentes. Pida siempre la comparación con una línea base sencilla.

Agroalimentario 12 casos de uso · 5 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve5 tendencias
  • El cuaderno de campo pasa a ser digital: la Orden APA/204/2023 fija el contenido del cuaderno digital de explotación agrícola (tratamientos fitosanitarios, abonado, semilla tratada) y hace obligatorio adjuntar el plan de abonado. Un registro digital ordenado es la base para cualquier ayuda de la IA.f4
  • La adopción de IA en la agricultura es desigual y los obstáculos pesan más en los actores pequeños: falta de datos de calidad, costes de desarrollo, falta de interoperabilidad e incertidumbre sobre el cumplimiento normativo, según el informe de la Comisión Europea de julio de 2025.f3
  • La explotación media de la UE es pequeña: cerca de 3 de cada 5 explotaciones tienen menos de 5 hectáreas. Las soluciones que valen para una finca grande no sirven sin adaptarse a una finca familiar pequeña.f1
  • El estudio del Parlamento Europeo señala que las herramientas basadas en datos funcionan mejor en explotaciones grandes con diseños estandarizados, y que habrá que desarrollar tecnología que funcione sin depender siempre de la nube ni de una buena conexión.f2
  • Riesgo específico del sector: quién es dueño de los datos de la explotación y quién depende de quién. El estudio del Parlamento Europeo advierte de que el agricultor puede acabar siendo dueño de su tierra pero alquilando sus datos y su equipo digital a grandes empresas. Antes de firmar con un proveedor: propiedad de los datos, derecho a llevárselos en un formato legible y plan B si falla la conexión.f2f5
Cifras4 cifras con fuente
  • 8,8 millones · Explotaciones agrarias en la UE, 2023f1
  • 62,8 % · Explotaciones de la UE con menos de 5 hectáreas, 2023 (dato provisional)f1
  • 17,8 ha · Tamaño medio de la explotación en la UE, 2023f1
  • 93 % · Explotaciones familiares en la UE, 2020f1

Asociaciones y tercer sector 10 casos de uso · 8 fuentes
Hacia dónde se mueve6 tendencias
  • El uso de IA ya es mayoritario en las entidades sociales británicas, aunque falta preparación: según el Charity Digital Skills Report 2026, el 79 % de las organizaciones benéficas usa IA, el 56 % dice que la falta de conocimientos es su mayor barrera y el 33 % afirma que su patronato tiene pocos conocimientos de IA.f3
  • La confianza es el punto débil: el 35 % de las organizaciones no se fía de las herramientas de IA, más del doble que el año anterior. Para una entidad que vive de la confianza de socios y donantes, el uso de IA debe poder explicarse.f3
  • Los financiadores también usan y notan la IA: el 58 % dice que la IA está cambiando las solicitudes que recibe y el 55 % no sabe si quienes solicitan la usan. Las solicitudes escritas con IA serán más habituales, pero los criterios de calidad y de veracidad no cambian.f3
  • Los reguladores piden responsabilidad humana y transparencia: la Charity Commission recuerda que los patronos siguen siendo responsables de las decisiones y que no deben delegarlas en la IA, y el Fundraising Regulator pide supervisión humana proporcionada, transparencia cuando el contenido pueda inducir a error a donantes o al público, y recomienda tener una política de IA.f1f2
  • En España, el tercer sector es grande y vive de las personas: en 2024 la Plataforma de ONG de Acción Social agrupó 36 organizaciones con 165.783 personas trabajadoras y 470.438 voluntarias. Una entidad pequeña puede copiar buenas prácticas, como la política interna de uso de IA que publicó la Plataforma del Voluntariado de España en 2026, con una lista de usos permitidos, supervisados y prohibidos.f4f5
  • Riesgo específico del sector: trabaja con personas en situación vulnerable y con datos sensibles. Los datos de salud o situación social son categorías especiales (RGPD y LOPDGDD), y los sistemas de IA que deciden el acceso a ayudas o servicios esenciales figuran entre los de alto riesgo del Reglamento de IA. Regla de partida: la IA ayuda a preparar; la decisión sobre una persona es siempre humana, y no se pegan datos personales en herramientas sin contrato ni base legal.f8f6f7f5
Cifras8 cifras con fuente
  • 79 % · Organizaciones benéficas británicas que usan IA, 2026f3
  • 56 % · Entidades que dicen que la falta de conocimientos es su mayor barrera para la IAf3
  • 35 % · Entidades que no se fían de las herramientas de IA (más del doble que el año anterior)f3

  • 55 % · Financiadores que no saben si quienes solicitan usan IAf3

  • 3.565.082 · Personas socias que colaboraron con esas entidades, 2024f4

Seguridad de la IA: compañías y soluciones (15 soluciones)

Lectura de mercado, no recomendación: compañías y soluciones que se presentan como respuesta a cada capacidad de seguridad de la IA del documento 35, con lo que dice de sí misma su página oficial, comprobada el 19-10-2026. SEVEN-G no evalúa, avala ni compara productos; la lista no es exhaustiva y se ordena alfabéticamente. Antes de usar cualquiera con datos de la compañía —también para probarla— se aplica la evaluación de proveedor (documento 36 y P55).

Guardarraíles en ejecución y pasarelas de IA 5 soluciones

Puntos de control fuera del modelo que filtran entradas, salidas y contexto, previenen fugas, aplican cuotas y registran el tráfico hacia los modelos.

Controles de SEVEN-G: SEG-26, SEG-03, SEG-07, AG-05

CompañíaSoluciónQué hace (según su página oficial)
Amazon Web ServicesAmazon Bedrock Guardrails1Salvaguardas configurables que detectan y filtran contenido dañino en texto e imágenes, ocultan información sensible y detectan alucinaciones del modelo.
CloudflareAI Gateway2Da visibilidad y control sobre las aplicaciones de IA: analítica, registro, caché, límites de uso y reintentos con un modelo alternativo.
Google CloudModel Armor3Revisa las instrucciones y las respuestas de los modelos de lenguaje para bloquear entradas maliciosas, contenido inseguro y fugas de datos sensibles.
MicrosoftAzure AI Content Safety (con Prompt Shields)4Detecta contenido dañino generado por usuarios y por IA en texto e imágenes; incluye Prompt Shields para detectar ataques de entrada contra un modelo de lenguaje.
NVIDIANeMo Guardrails5Biblioteca de Python de acceso abierto para añadir comprobaciones de seguridad y de política a aplicaciones de modelos de lenguaje, sobre las instrucciones y las respuestas, sin cambiar el modelo.

Fuentes

  2. Cloudflare AI Gateway · Cloudflare (s. f.)
  3. Model Armor overview · Google Cloud (s. f.)
  4. What is Azure AI Content Safety? - Azure AI services | Microsoft Learn · Microsoft (s. f.)
  5. Overview · NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails library · NVIDIA (s. f.)

El cliente agéntico: compañías y soluciones (23 soluciones)

Lectura de mercado, no recomendación: compañías, protocolos y soluciones que se presentan como respuesta a alguna de las cuatro caras del cliente agéntico (documento 35, sección 9.4), con lo que dice de sí misma su página oficial, comprobada el 15-11-2026. Los protocolos en borrador se citan como orientación y no fundamentan ningún control. SEVEN-G no evalúa, avala ni compara productos; la lista no es exhaustiva y se ordena alfabéticamente. Antes de usar cualquiera con datos de la compañía —también para probarla— se aplica la evaluación de proveedor (documento 36 y P55).

Aviso legal y exención de responsabilidad

SEVEN-G y esta herramienta se ofrecen «tal cual» y con fines exclusivamente informativos. No constituyen asesoramiento jurídico, regulatorio, financiero ni profesional, ni garantizan el cumplimiento de ninguna norma. Los criterios, clasificaciones y referencias a regulación general (Reglamento Europeo de IA, RGPD, DORA, NIS2…) o sectorial pueden ser incompletos, no aplicar a un caso concreto o quedar desactualizados por cambios normativos. Cada organización que use la herramienta es la única responsable de identificar la normativa que le aplica, verificar su vigencia y certificar su propio cumplimiento regulatorio, con el asesoramiento cualificado que corresponda. Esta metodología es una ayuda genérica y gratuita, compartida con la comunidad para que nadie tenga que empezar desde cero; cada persona u organización puede y debe adaptarla a su propio uso. No debe entenderse que sus partes jurídicamente sensibles hayan sido revisadas por una asesoría jurídica: esas revisiones, para cada empresa o sector, son responsabilidad última de la empresa, el consultor o la organización que la use. Aunque se procura mantenerla al día, alguna norma puede haber cambiado sin que se recoja aquí. En la máxima medida permitida por la ley, el autor no asume responsabilidad alguna por los efectos de su aplicación en ninguna organización ni por su aplicabilidad completa. La metodología no otorga certificación de ningún tipo. El autor no asume responsabilidad alguna por el uso de la herramienta ni por las decisiones adoptadas con ella. Los datos de demostración son ficticios. Las cifras y tendencias de mercado son de sus fuentes, que se citan, y pueden haber cambiado desde su publicación.

Gallery of examples by sectorWhat the use case register and the board dashboard of a company in your sector could look like, and where AI use cases are heading

What it is for: to start from something close to your reality rather than from scratch. Each example is a complete T01 use case register of a fictitious company in the sector (phases, gate decisions, expected and realised value, risks and closures) and the board dashboard that T17 generates from it. Below, for 30 sectors, what companies are adopting now and which high-value use cases are expected in 2027-2028, not only generative AI: also predictive ML, RPA and IDP, computer vision, optimisation and sector-specific tools, with their sources.

Companies, people, suppliers and figures are fictitious and have been built so as not to resemble any real organisation; any resemblance is coincidental. The use cases in each example draw on what the market is adopting according to the sources in the next section.

Where each sector is heading (505 use cases, 221 sources)

A reading of recent public studies, surveys and reports: primary or official sources only, all in the SEVEN-G reference register and checked. Use cases are grouped by horizon: established (common practice in the sector), being adopted (rolling out in 2025-2026) and emerging 2027-2028 (where the sources expect the next jump in value). They are guidance for prioritising with the sphere map (document 10) and the T01 register, not a recommendation for any specific company.

How to read it. Open a sector. Inside, “Where it is heading”, “Figures” and each use case are cards: opening one closes the others. Each case carries three tags: the technology, the SPHERES sphere where it usually creates value and the ambition level (optimise, augment, transform or enablement). Sphere and level are indicative: they are derived from the function and the lever of the case, and the same case can be framed with more or less ambition in your company. Opening the card shows the usual techniques for that technology and the sources for the case.

Banking 24 use cases · 11 sources

Register and dashboard example for this sector: in the gallery above.

Where it is heading6 trends
  • Predictive ML is established and in production across European banking: customer and transaction profiling, customer support, fraud, AML/CFT, credit scoring and credit risk models. Few banks remain in pilots and in-house development is growing.f4f6f8
  • Generative and agentic AI now account for most new deployments announced by large banks; developer augmentation has become table stakes.f1f2f3f9
  • Value measurement remains the exception: few use cases disclose impact metrics, although reports of revenue uplift (conversion, cross-sell, acquisition) are growing alongside efficiency.f2f9
  • AI agents are entering compliance and operations first (KYC, source of wealth, fraud claims, collections) under human oversight; full autonomy remains marginal.f1f7f10f11
  • Regulatory pressure centres on governance: the AI Act classifies creditworthiness assessment as high-risk and supervisors focus on AI policies, explainability, human oversight and third-party dependency.f5f6f7
  • 2026-2028 horizon: customers' own AI agents may become a channel that compares, switches products and moves balances, pressuring deposits and margins and forcing a rethink of distribution.f9f10
Figures13 sourced figures

Real-time payment fraud detectionPredictive ML07 · DecisionOptimise

ML models (decision trees, neural networks) score every card payment and transfer and block or escalate suspicious ones within milliseconds.f4f6f8

Function
Risk
Value lever
Risk and compliance
Technology and usual techniques
Predictive ML. Models that learn from historical data with a known outcome. Most used with tabular data: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), random forests and logistic regression as an explainable baseline. For anomalies: isolation forests or autoencoders. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

Insurance 24 use cases · 12 sources

Register and dashboard example for this sector: in the gallery above.

Where it is heading8 trends
  • 'Traditional' ML is mature in non-life: pricing, fraud, claims management, renewal churn and cross-sell; life lags behind. In-house builds with human oversight and challenger models in pricing prevail.f3f5
  • Generative AI is being adopted fast but cautiously: two in three European insurers use it, mostly in back office (document extraction, drafting, code, underwriting support), and most use cases are still proofs of concept.f1f2
  • The bottleneck is scaling and measuring: few insurers have scaled AI, many do not measure outcomes, and spending goes to technology rather than change management.f6f9
  • Claims and underwriting hold the automation gap: straight-through processing is partial in personal-lines underwriting and the vast majority of claims still involve significant manual work; core-system modernisation is a prerequisite.f8f9f10
  • 2026-2028 horizon: insurers expect a considerable rise in agentic AI (today a small fraction of use cases), first in simple claims, commercial underwriting and portfolio management.f2f7f10
  • Trust and regulation set the pace: the AI Act treats life and health risk assessment and pricing as high-risk, EIOPA asks for proportionate governance, and customers accept AI but want human contact and distrust agent recommendations.f4f2f11
  • Data-driven product models (telematics, parametric) remain a minority but are the growth path tied to IoT and climate risks.f3
  • The gap between ambition and results remains open: in a 2026 study, only 18% of insurance executives say they have a view of AI shared by their executive team, and 45% leave AI with the technology function alone. About half of the AI budget goes to internal efficiency and between 5% and 10% to new products or revenue. The study proposes measuring by business outcomes, not headcount reduction. Its sample is small (44 executives from 20 countries).f12
Figures17 sourced figures
  • ~65 % · European insurers already using generative AI (plus 23% planning to within three years)f2
  • 64 % / 36 % · Internal vs customer-facing generative AI use cases (957 reported)f2
  • 32 % · Generative AI use cases already in productionf2
  • 9 % · Agentic generative AI use cases today (a considerable rise expected within three years); assisted and semi-autonomous total 83%f2
  • 40 % / 32 % / 22 % · Insurers already using generative AI in customer service / claims / distributionf2
  • 64 % / 59 % / 54 % · Insurers planning generative AI within three years in fraud / claims / distributionf2
  • 49 % · Insurers with a dedicated AI policy (25% in 2023)f1
  • 59 % / 30 % · European consumers wary of AI-agent recommendations for choosing insurance or pensions vs those who would trust themf2
  • 50 % / 24 % · Insurers using AI (any type) in non-life / lifef3
  • 17 % / ~10 % · Insurers offering telematics motor / parametric productsf3
  • 95 % · UK insurers already using AI (highest adoption of any sector)f5
  • 7 % · Insurers that have scaled their AI systemsf6
  • ~5.000 M€ · Annual automation efficiency pool for European insurers (P&C ~€3bn, life ~€1bn, health ~€0.5bn)f8
  • >90 % · Claim events still processed with significant manual involvementf8
  • ~42 %; 72 % / 28 % · P&C insurers that have not measured AI outcomes; AI spend split technology / change managementf9
  • hasta 160.000 M USD · Potential P&C savings from real-time fraud analytics by 2032 (global)f10
  • ~70 % · Customers who have used general-purpose generative AI tools on their own when buying insurancef11

Manufacturing 24 use cases · 11 sources

Register and dashboard example for this sector: in the gallery above.

Where it is heading9 trends
  • Analytical AI and ML remain the backbone of plant value: at reference factories (Lighthouses) they underpin about 62% of the top-five solutions, while generative AI rose from 9% (2024) to 23% (2025).f1f2
  • AI agents are starting to appear in production (5% of Lighthouse solutions in 2025), almost always with a human in the loop and autonomy graded by decision risk; full autonomy in production is still considered theoretical.f1
  • Shift from 'smart factory' to 'cognitive factory' and 'cognitive networks': orchestrator agents coordinating task agents, AI models and RPA across the value chain (planning, procurement, production, logistics and after-sales).f1f7f3
  • Value concentrates in function-specific vertical applications (planning, quality, procurement, R&D, service) rather than horizontal copilots; the most frequent use cases remain predictive maintenance, production scheduling and process improvement.f1f2
  • The bottleneck is no longer technology but scaling: legacy IT/OT data and systems, talent and cybersecurity. Leaders invest first in foundations (data, cloud, IIoT) before advanced AI.f4f1
  • Physical AI (AI-guided robots and automation) and simulation make full plant redesign economically viable; BCG estimates productivity gains of up to 60% and argues upgrading can compete with offshoring.f6f3
  • After-sales services and installed-base monitoring emerge as an agent-supported revenue source (wear detection, parts ordering, service scheduling).f3
  • In the EU adoption is still moderate: 17.3% of manufacturing enterprises with 10+ employees used AI in 2025 (19.95% overall), with large gaps by subsector (pharma 41%, electronics 37%, food 12%).f5
  • Public policy is pushing sector adoption: the European Commission's Apply AI Strategy includes manufacturing among its priority sectors, with digital twins and experience centres for SMEs.f10

Predictive maintenance of critical equipmentPredictive ML04 · OperationsOptimise

ML models on sensor data (vibration, temperature, power draw) anticipate failures and schedule intervention before breakdown.f2f1

Function
Maintenance
Value lever
Efficiency
Technology and usual techniques
Predictive ML. Models that learn from historical data with a known outcome. Most used with tabular data: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), random forests and logistic regression as an explainable baseline. For anomalies: isolation forests or autoencoders. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

Public sector 23 use cases · 10 sources

Register and dashboard example for this sector: in the gallery above.

Where it is heading8 trends
  • AI is now almost universal across OECD governments, but concentrated in internal processes and public services; use in policymaking and oversight remains a minority.f1
  • Generative AI is mostly used in low-risk, productivity-enhancing applications (staff assistance, summaries, drafting), not in high-stakes operational decisions.f1f7
  • Pilots proliferate but rarely scale: few countries measure the financial or non-financial impact of use cases, and operational controls (pre-deployment assessment, post-deployment audit, algorithm registers) lag.f1f2
  • In Europe most observed cases target internal management and operational efficiency; chatbots and virtual assistants are a prominent family and AI dominates other emerging technologies.f3
  • The next step is agentic AI applied to routine decisions, with growing requirements for explainability and human-in-the-loop in decisions affecting citizens.f4f5
  • Data readiness, security and trust in outputs are the main barriers, ahead of technology.f5f6f4
  • Governments are investing in in-house and sovereign tools (shared AI platforms, internal tools such as the UK Humphrey programme) and reusable cross-cutting use cases.f8f9
  • The EU AI Act classifies common government uses as high-risk (access to essential public services and benefits, employment, migration, justice); obligations for these systems apply from 2 December 2027 following the Omnibus amendment.f10
Figures10 sourced figures
  • 35 de 36 (97 %) · OECD countries using AI in at least one area of government (2025)f1
  • 70 % → 86 % · OECD countries using AI for internal processes (2023 → 2025)f1
  • 67 % → 75 % · OECD countries using AI in public services (2023 → 2025)f1
  • 64 % · OECD countries using generative AI for at least one purposef1
  • 28 % (10 de 36) · OECD countries reporting any financial or non-financial impact measurement of AI use casesf1
  • 17 % (6 de 36) · OECD countries with an open algorithm registerf1
  • 87 % / 20 % · Share of 2025 European public-sector emerging-tech cases that are AI / of which chatbots or virtual assistantsf3
  • al menos 80 % · Governments expected to deploy AI agents to automate routine decision-making by 2028 (prediction)f4
  • 90 % / 21 % · Public-sector organisations planning to explore, pilot or implement agentic AI within 2-3 years / with the data needed to train or fine-tune modelsf5
  • 26 minutos al día · Time saved per civil servant with a generative AI office assistant (20,000-person trial)f7

Function

Value lever
Revenue
Technology and usual techniques
Predictive ML. Models that learn from historical data with a known outcome. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

Energy 25 use cases · 12 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • The power grid is the main AI frontier in energy: fault detection and location, dynamic line rating and grid-enhancing technologies that squeeze more out of existing lines while physical expansion is delayed by equipment and connection lead times.f2f1f5f4
  • Dual relationship 'energy for AI' and 'AI for energy': data-centre growth drives demand-forecasting uncertainty and requires new forecasting, flexibility and connection-planning tools.f5f7f2
  • Real adoption is still partial: 45% of utilities use AI for grid optimisation, but only 16% have implemented advanced power-flow and resilience approaches; lack of digital skills is the main barrier.f7f3
  • In control rooms AI advances as decision support, not autonomous control: generative copilots for operators and technicians, with model registries, audit trails and risk controls.f5
  • Oil and gas, an early adopter, is shifting IT spend towards AI (up to half by 2029) and combining physics-based models with AI in well optimisation, refining, asset integrity and crude supply chains.f6f1f12
  • The EU makes AI in energy explicit policy: digitalisation and AI roadmap (June 2026) focused on grid optimisation, demand-side flexibility, data-centre integration and European foundation models for grids (AI.grids).f4
  • EU energy companies are among the heaviest AI users (33.6% vs 20% overall) and cybersecurity is their top use, as cyberattacks on utilities have tripled in four years.f9f10f2
  • Methane and emissions: satellite observation multiplies leak detection and quantification capacity, with large abatement potential at no net cost.f11

Renewable generation forecastingPredictive ML04 · OperationsOptimise

ML models using weather and plant data forecast wind and solar output to schedule, cut curtailment and reduce fossil backup.f2f1

Function
Operations
Value lever
Sustainability
Technology and usual techniques
Predictive ML. Models that learn from historical data with a known outcome. Most used with tabular data: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), random forests and logistic regression as an explainable baseline. For anomalies: isolation forests or autoencoders. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

Logistics and transport 24 use cases · 11 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • Wide gap between ambition and results: 97% of logistics executives see AI as a strategic priority, but only 13% say it already delivers financial results; most are still exploring or testing.f1f2
  • Real adoption concentrates on transport planning and optimisation, tracking and visibility, demand forecasting, route optimisation and automated customer service.f2f1
  • AI already influences buying decisions: 40% of shippers consider AI capabilities when choosing a logistics provider, and 93% of providers see competitive risk from AI-native entrants.f2f1
  • Documentation (bids, customs, contracts, invoices) is the fastest ground for generative AI and agents, with full payback in 18-24 months among adopters.f3f1f6
  • Towards the agentic supply chain: agents that detect capacity gaps, request carrier bids, book within guardrails and reroute shipments during disruptions; agent governance is the weak point.f5f4f7
  • Regulatory digitalisation opens room for document automation: the EU eFTI Regulation requires authorities to accept electronic freight information from 9 July 2027.f8
  • AI adoption in EU transport and storage is among the lowest (11.2% of enterprises in 2025 vs 20% overall), leaving room for differentiation for early scalers.f9
  • Warehouse robotics and physical AI advance alongside software AI; fleet energy efficiency (routing, maintenance, driving) adds a sustainability lever.f1f11

Retail and consumer goods 24 use cases · 10 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • AI is moving from pilots into core operations: two in three retail executives expect to adopt agentic AI within 12-24 months and almost all retailers are exploring or implementing agents.f1f5
  • AI assistants are becoming a discovery and purchase channel (agentic commerce): traffic from generative assistants is growing and visibility in their answers requires machine-readable catalogues (generative experience optimisation, GXO).f1f3f5
  • Consumers are adopting AI for shopping but demand control: they want clear rules on when an assistant acts and worry about how their data is used.f2f4
  • Merchandising is shifting to always-on pricing, promotion, assortment and inventory agents; decisions that took weeks now take hours.f7f8
  • Operating model shift: category managers act as AI-supported 'mini CEOs', above-store productivity rises and capex moves to supply chain automation, AI platforms and data.f6
  • Strategic divergence: 'destination' retailers monetise owned data through loyalty, personalisation and retail media; 'evaluation' retailers reached via AI platforms face margin pressure.f6
  • New-generation, agentic-AI-enabled supply chains are among executives' top technology priorities.f9
  • Risk is shifting from shoplifting to fraud schemes (phone scams, loyalty, gift cards) and retailers are investing in risk-intelligence technologies.f10
Figures13 sourced figures
  • 68 % · Retail executives expecting agentic AI adoption within 12-24 months (survey of 330 executives)f1
  • 67 % · Executives expecting AI-driven personalisation capabilities within the next yearf1
  • hasta el 25 % / up to 25% · Forecast influence of AI agents on global e-commerce sales by 2030f1
  • 25 % (y otro 31 % prevé usarlas) · Consumers who used Gen AI shopping tools in 2025 (12,000 consumers, 12 countries)f2
  • 76 % · Consumers wanting clear rules for when an AI assistant actsf2
  • 58 % · Consumers who replaced traditional search engines with Gen AI for product recommendations (25% in 2023)f3
  • 45 % · Consumers turning to AI during their buying journey (18,000 consumers, 23 countries)f4
  • 4.700 % · Year-on-year growth in traffic to US retail sites from Gen AI browsers and chat services (July 2025, Adobe data cited by BCG)f5
  • 96 % · Surveyed retailers exploring or implementing AI agentsf5
  • 5-10 % · Gross profit increase at retailers implementing AI-powered pricingf8
  • > 30 % · Above-store productivity increase in AI-mature organisationsf6
  • 67 % · Executives who believe agentic AI will boost supply chain productivity (1,000 executives)f9
  • 61 % · Retailers investing in risk-intelligence technologies against retail crime; shoplifting incidents fell 12.4% in 2025f10

Telecommunications 24 use cases · 12 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • Efficiency remains the main driver: most operators deploy AI in the network primarily to cut operating costs.f6f1
  • Autonomous networks: most operators sit at levels 1-3, but a growing number declare and validate level 4 in specific network domains and aim to scale it before 2030.f1f5f11
  • From copilot to agent: AI agents are spreading across customer care, network operations and IT, with the 'AI-first telco' as the target and a strong EBITDA uplift.f2f4
  • Service assurance is becoming customer-centric: fraud, security, care and network optimisation today; automated complaint and fault resolution and network health prediction next.f7
  • New AI revenue streams: network APIs, AI-optimised connectivity, cloud and edge, cybersecurity services and GPU-as-a-service.f3f8
  • In Europe, operators already offer AI services (infrastructure, models, data, applications) and lead in network API announcements, with edge nodes and own data centres.f8
  • AI risk is rising on the agenda: operators lag other sectors in responsible AI methodologies, and trust and privacy top their risk list.f9
  • Customer value is shifting: reward programmes may matter as much as network performance, reinforcing personalised customer value management.f10f2
Figures12 sourced figures
  • 85 % · Operators citing opex efficiency as a priority objective for AI in networks (100 operators)f6
  • 20 % · Operators reporting level 4 or 5 autonomy in select domains; 35% expect to reach it within two yearsf1
  • ≈ 30 % · Opex savings operators are targeting from autonomous networks by 2028f1
  • 84 % · Operators at autonomy level 1 or 2 across their overall network; over 60% aim for level 3+ by 2028f5
  • 1,7x - 3,4x · Return on autonomous network projects (conservative to optimistic), with 2.9 to 1.5-year paybackf5
  • +15 p.p. · EBITDA uplift of an 'AI-first' telco (and +10 pp EBIT)f2
  • 45-60 % / 40-50 % · Productivity gain in customer care / network operations in an 'AI-first' telcof2
  • 30.000 M$ a > 300.000 M$ · Estimated global network API revenues by 2030f3
  • x5 · Digital sales multiplier at an operator whose agentic assistants send 40,000+ messages a dayf4
  • 38 % · European share of global network API announcements (2025)f8
  • 5.300 M€ · European operators' cybersecurity revenues in 2025 (EUR 3.2bn in 2020)f8
  • 59 % · Telcos with a robust methodology to manage AI risks (66% across all sectors)f9

Healthcare 21 use cases · 11 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • AI-assisted diagnostics (mainly imaging) is the most widespread clinical use in European health systems, followed by patient-facing chatbots.f1f6
  • Ambient clinical documentation (transcription and summarisation of consultations) moves from pilot to scaled rollout in 2026, with specific guidance on clinical safety, data protection and medical-device regulation.f2f3
  • Waiting-list pressure steers AI towards access and patient flow: digital triage, no-show reduction and tools to manage urgent and planned care.f2f5
  • Scaled adoption remains limited and returns are rarely measured: many providers run generative AI at scale only in selected areas and half have not yet measured results.f7
  • Executives expect value from agentic AI as early as 2026 and prioritise it for clinical operations, care delivery and revenue cycle, with cost-saving expectations over 2-3 years.f11
  • Governance lags: few countries have a health-specific AI strategy; legal uncertainty and affordability are barriers, while dedicated AI and data roles in health are growing.f1
  • Large multimodal models open new clinical uses, but their ability to perform a wide range of health tasks is not yet proven and they require specific governance.f9
  • In the EU, AI that is (or is part of) a regulated medical device is high-risk; after the Omnibus amendment, those obligations apply from 2 August 2028, and those for Annex III uses (e.g. access to essential services such as healthcare) from 2 December 2027.f8
Figures10 sourced figures
  • más del 80 % · US health technology executives expecting moderate-to-significant value from agentic AI in 2026f11
  • 74 % · EU Member States using AI in diagnosticsf1
  • 63 % · EU Member States using chatbots for patient engagementf1
  • 30 % / 2 % · Surveyed health systems operating generative AI at scale in selected areas / enterprise-widef7
  • 51 % · Health executives who have not yet measured AI returns or consider it prematuref7
  • 47 minutos por turno · Time saved by ambient documentation in the emergency department (St George's pilot)f2
  • más de 9.000 · Extra daily A&E consultations if ambient documentation were scaled to 11,000+ clinicians in England (modelling)f2
  • 30 % · Reduction in missed appointments with AI prediction and back-up bookings (6-month pilot)f5
  • 41.000 M£ (sobre 10.000 M£ de inversión en tres años) · Total expected benefits of the NHS technology, data and AI investment over ten yearsf2
  • 75 % · Public healthcare organisations exploring or deploying generative AIf10

Where it is heading8 trends
  • Regulators are converging on a common frame: in January 2026 EMA and FDA agreed ten good AI practice principles for the whole medicines lifecycle (research, trials, manufacturing and safety monitoring).f2
  • The regulatory approach is risk-proportionate: validation and model-credibility requirements rise when AI affects patient safety or regulatory decisions (e.g. posology or treatment assignment).f1f3
  • The largest potential value of generative AI lies in early research and clinical development: target assessment, in silico screening, trial document drafting and faster enrolment.f6
  • Scaling remains limited: a minority report having scaled AI successfully and few see significant returns, while agentic AI emerges as a new area of interest.f7
  • Agencies themselves are adopting generative and agentic AI for scientific review, label comparison, safety surveillance and inspections, raising the speed and standard of interactions with industry.f4f5
  • In GMP manufacturing, AI focuses on image-based quality control, process monitoring (CQA/CPP), predictive maintenance and deviation analysis, with current GMP frameworks as the validation basis.f9
  • Practical governance (AI inventory, computerised system validation, traceability and training) is what unlocks use cases in pharmacovigilance, trials and quality.f8
  • The EU AI Act mainly affects AI embedded in medical devices (obligations from 2 August 2028 after the Omnibus amendment); industry holds that AI used solely for medicines R&D is exempt.f10f8

Travel and hospitality 25 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • The sector is late but accelerating fast: large travel companies mentioning AI in annual reports rose from 4% (2022) to 35% (2024), and AI now attracts about half of travel start-up funding.f7f8
  • Travellers plan with generative AI but rarely delegate booking: trust in AI information is high while permission to book is very low.f5f6f7
  • Distribution is being reshaped: hotels compete to appear in AI assistants' recommendation lists, and agentic AI may disintermediate or strengthen large platforms, with SMEs at risk of losing visibility.f2f3f1
  • Labour pressure drives operational AI: staff shortages and rising labour costs push automation of housekeeping, scheduling, procurement and energy in hotels.f2f3
  • In airlines, the 'AI-first' model integrates commercial and operations: network and pricing simulation, predictive maintenance, operations control and personalised retailing.f4
  • Destinations and governments use AI for demand forecasting, visitor flow management, reducing seasonality and sustainability, though tourism-specific AI strategies remain rare.f1f9
  • Rising risks: fake reviews, fabricated offers, algorithmic bias in pricing and recommendations, and adoption and skills gaps between SMEs and large firms.f1f2
  • Travellers want single platforms integrating flights, accommodation, activities and payments, a natural ground for end-to-end travel agents.f8f4
Figures12 sourced figures

  • > 90 % frente a 2 % · Consumers trusting AI-generated travel information versus those letting AI bookf7

  • 94 % · Industry leaders who see AI as mission-critical; 91% plan to increase tech investmentf8
  • 39 % · SMEs (all sectors, 10 countries) using some form of AI in 2025 (26% in 2024)f1

SMEs, professional firms and local businesses

Cases designed for companies without an IT team: inexpensive tools or ones already included in what is used, with professional risk (professional secrecy, data protection, human oversight and the EU AI Act) in view. Start with “Use cases that fit almost any business”; then open your sector, which only adds what is specific to it.

Use cases that fit almost any business 14 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • Small businesses already use AI, but still a minority: 17% of small EU enterprises and 21.4% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees use it. Starting now is not late, but it is no longer a pioneer's move.f1f2
  • The most common uses are selling and administering: 34.7% of EU enterprises using AI apply it to marketing or sales and 31.1% to organising administration or management. They are also the cheapest cases to start with.f1
  • There is public funding to digitalise a business: the Kit Digital programme catalogue includes e-invoicing, social media management, customer management and e-commerce solutions, with maximum aid per category. Before signing anything, check on the official site which calls are open and for which company size.f5
  • Delegating to an AI assistant requires control: the Spanish data protection authority proposes five questions before delegating (what it can see, what it can remember, what it can do on my behalf, where it sends the data and whether it affects anyone else), minimum permissions and confirmation before sending, sharing, paying or contracting.f4
  • Specific risk for small businesses: AI with customer and employee data needs a legal basis, a contract with the provider and human review. Article 4 of the AI Act requires training the staff who use AI, and systems for selecting or scoring candidates may be high-risk.f6f7f9f8
Figures7 sourced figures
  • 17 % · Small (10-49) EU enterprises using AI, 2025f1
  • 34,7 % / 31,1 % · EU enterprises using AI for marketing or sales / for organising administration or managementf1
  • 21,36 % · Spanish enterprises with fewer than 10 employees using AI (Q1 2026)f2
  • 5 · Questions proposed by the Spanish data protection authority before delegating tasks to an AI assistant or agentf4
  • 2-08-2026 · Date from which supervision of the AI literacy obligation in Article 4 of the AI Act startsf7
  • 3.000 € · Maximum Kit Digital catalogue aid for billing and e-invoicingf5
  • 5.000 € · Maximum Kit Digital catalogue aid for social media managementf5

Management and strategy consulting 14 use cases · 6 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Inside what AI does well, consultants gain a lot; outside it, they err more. In an experiment with 758 consultants, those using generative AI on a creative task reached a level 40% higher, but on a business problem-solving task outside the tool's competence they were 23% less likely to be correct than those without it.f1
  • AI is already entering the firm without anyone approving it: 78% of AI users at work bring their own tools, and 80% in small and medium companies. For a small consultancy the risk is client-confidential information ending up in tools with no contract or control.f2f6
  • Adoption in the companies they advise is still a minority and uneven by size: in the EU 17% of small enterprises (10-49 people), 30.4% of medium and 55% of large ones use AI; in Spain, 21.4% of those with fewer than 10 employees. That is the market gap for a consultancy that can implement AI in SMEs.f3f4
  • Enterprises already using AI apply it mainly to marketing or sales (34.7%) and to organising business administration or management (31.1%): these are the first two fronts where they will ask the consultancy for diagnosis, prioritisation and support.f3
  • The consultant's value shifts from the product (the report) to judgement: choosing what to automate, verifying what the machine produces and answering for the result. Client trust requires traceability of which part of a deliverable is generated and who reviewed it.f1f2
  • Regulatory and data risk: when the consultancy processes client personal data with AI it normally acts as a processor (GDPR), and if it implements AI systems for a client it should check whether they fall into the high-risk categories of the AI Act.f6f5

IT integrators and services 13 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Software development is where AI is most widespread: 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools and 51% of professionals use them daily, but more distrust their accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%).f2
  • Measured results are promising but bounded: in a controlled trial with 95 professional developers, those using a coding assistant finished one specific task 55% faster. The task was narrow and does not equal a whole working day.f1
  • AI amplifies what is already there: the 2025 DORA report concludes that its main role is that of an amplifier of an organisation's strengths and weaknesses. An integrator with orderly testing and delivery processes benefits; one without multiplies disorder.f3
  • AI agents are not yet mainstream: only 14.1% of respondents use them daily and 37.9% do not plan to. For the small integrator they are a path to managed services, not a mature product.f2
  • SME client demand is growing but readiness is low: 17% of small EU enterprises and 21.4% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees use AI, and shadow AI is common (80% in SMEs). The integrator is usually the one who ends up configuring permissions, data and security.f4f5f6
  • Product and service security becomes a legal duty: the Cyber Resilience Act sets security requirements for products with digital elements, and the GDPR and the AI Act affect what the integrator deploys for clients. Contracts and responsibilities must say who answers for what.f8f9f7
Figures8 sourced figures

  • ≈ 55 % más rápido · Speed on a bounded programming task with an AI assistant versus without (95 developers)f1
  • 80 % · AI users bringing their own tools to work in SMEsf6
  • 17 % · Small (10-49) EU enterprises using AI, 2025 (medium: 30.4%; large: 55%)f4
  • 21,36 % · Spanish enterprises with fewer than 10 employees using AI (INE, Q1 2026)f5

Most used with tabular data: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), random forests and logistic regression as an explainable baseline. For anomalies: isolation forests or autoencoders. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

Engineering, installation and construction projects 15 use cases · 6 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Actual adoption is low and expectation high: in a survey of more than 2,200 professionals, about 45% had no AI implemented and just under 12% used it regularly in specific processes.f1
  • The brakes are practical, not technological: lack of skilled staff (46%), integration with existing systems (37%) and data quality and availability (30%). For an SME, organising project data comes before any tool.f1
  • Expected use in design and engineering is growing: about 35% of infrastructure and building professionals expect more than half of their projects to use AI within three years, but more than a third of firms have limited or no controls to manage AI risk in design and construction.f2
  • Professional risk is not delegated: a calculation, measurement or design generated with AI is signed and answered for by a technical person. Firms also cite data risks (intellectual property, privacy and cybersecurity) at around one in five.f2
  • Across the economy 17% of small EU enterprises and 21.4% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees use AI: the installation or engineering SME that gets organised early gains an edge in quotes, tenders and schedules.f3f4
  • Regulation to watch: the GDPR reaches cameras, drones and records of people on site, and some AI systems managing critical infrastructure may be high-risk under the AI Act; check before purchasing them.f6f5

Administrative and labour gestorías 14 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Invoicing is being digitalised by law and the gestoría will be the one to implement it: Royal Decree 1007/2023 and Order HAC/1177/2024 regulate the requirements of invoicing software (Veri*factu), and the Tax Agency has announced an extension of the adaptation deadline.f3
  • Europe is moving to structured invoices: Directive (EU) 2025/516 lets Member States require e-invoicing and sets near-real-time information systems for cross-border B2B transactions from 1 July 2030 and, as the deadline for national systems, 1 January 2035. Structured data means more automation is possible.f4
  • The tax authority also uses AI, always under human oversight: the 2025 Tax and Customs Control Plan guidelines announce the study of AI projects across the Tax Agency's areas of action without letting AI be the last decision instance. Expect more data cross-checks and automated requests.f5
  • Professionals expect to save about five hours a week with AI, but only 22% of organisations have a defined, visible AI strategy; those that do are twice as likely to see revenue growth.f6
  • Its clients are SMEs and micro-businesses: 17% of small EU enterprises and 21.4% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees use AI. The gestoría can be the natural channel through which clients adopt AI in an orderly, controlled way.f1f2
  • Specific risk for labour gestorías: payroll, sick leave and health data are special-category personal data (GDPR and LOPDGDD), and AI systems for recruiting, evaluating or managing people are among the high-risk ones in the AI Act. Before using a tool with employee data: legal basis, processor contract and human review.f9f7f8
Figures8 sourced figures
  • 17 % · Small (10-49) EU enterprises using AI, 2025f1
  • 34,7 % / 31,1 % · EU enterprises using AI for marketing or sales / for organising administration or managementf1
  • 21,36 % · Spanish enterprises with fewer than 10 employees using AI (Q1 2026)f2
  • 5 horas · Weekly saving professionals expect from AI over the next yearf6
  • 22 % · Organisations with a visible, defined AI strategyf6
  • 53 % · Professionals whose organisations already see ROI from AIf6
  • 1-07-2030 · Date of near-real-time information systems for cross-border B2B transactions (ViDA)f4

Law firms 15 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • In Spain AI is already in most of the firms that answered, but with little knowledge: in the Spanish General Council of the Bar survey (1,841 responses, almost 80% from sole or small practices) 58.9% use AI tools, 49.1% report low knowledge and 11.6% none; 65% want training. The authors warn that the sample is concentrated in a few bar associations.f1
  • Uses are instrumental: virtual assistants or chatbots, transcription and scheduling in firm management; assisted drafting, summaries and translation for documents; and monitoring of regulatory changes and predictive analysis in legal support. Automatic contract generation is still incipient.f1
  • The central risk is the convincing error: in a Stanford study, the AI legal research tools of two major publishers gave incorrect information in more than 17% and more than 34% of queries, and general chatbots hallucinated between 58% and 82% on legal queries.f5
  • Responsibility is personal and already written down: the interpretive circular to the Code of Ethics approved on 10 April 2026 treats AI as an auxiliary tool subject to human supervision, requires reading everything generated in full, checking it against reliable legal sources and keeping a trace of when and for what it was used; the infraction is complete when the erroneous document is filed.f2
  • The Spanish Bar's ten-principle decalogue (28 May 2026) adds effective human control, personal responsibility, that the client knows when automated tools are involved, confidentiality and security, bias prevention and continuing training.f3
  • Professional secrecy determines where AI runs: the Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe technical guide (27 March 2026) compares on-premises, self-hosted, rented infrastructure and vendor-hosted services, and notes that the less control you have over the stack, the more you must rely on enforceable contracts, and verify they are enforceable.f4
  • Professionals expect to save about five hours a week with AI, but only 22% of organisations have a defined strategy; a small firm gains more from a simple policy than from many tools.f6
  • Accompanying legal framework: the GDPR and the LOPDGDD require a legal basis and a processor contract before pouring client data into a tool, and the AI Act requires each firm to know in what role (deployer, provider) it acts with each system.f9f7f8
Figures9 sourced figures
  • 1 841 · Responses to the Spanish General Council of the Bar survey on AIf1
  • 58,9 % · Respondents currently using AI tools in practice (with the survey's own caveats)f1
  • 49,1 % / 11,6 % · Respondents with low / no knowledge of AI applied to lawf1
  • 65,0 % · Respondents interested in specific trainingf1
  • ≈ 80 % · Responses coming from sole or small practicesf1
  • > 17 % · Incorrect answers from an AI legal research tool (Lexis+ AI)f5
  • > 34 % · Incorrect answers from another AI legal research tool (Westlaw AI-Assisted Research)f5
  • 58 %-82 % · Hallucinations by general-purpose chatbots on legal queriesf5
  • 5 horas · Weekly saving professionals expect from AI over the next yearf6

Tax and accounting advisory firms 15 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading8 trends
  • The size gap is clear: according to ACCA, over 40% of large corporates use AI for data analysis and reporting, against less than 30% of sole practitioners and small or medium-sized practices, and the report warns that the gap may widen unless access is democratised.f1
  • The small practice's obstacle is not willingness but choosing well: small practices and sole practitioners are more daunted by identifying and selecting the right solution, and ask for accessible solutions designed for their size.f1
  • Professionals expect to save about five hours a week; in the US a combined annual impact of $32 billion is estimated for the legal and accounting sectors. Organisations with a defined AI strategy are twice as likely to see revenue growth, but only 22% have one.f2
  • Invoicing is being regulated as software: Royal Decree 1007/2023 and Order HAC/1177/2024 set requirements for invoicing software (Veri*factu) and the Tax Agency has announced an extension of the deadline. Every client with invoicing software is both a service opportunity and a compliance risk.f3
  • Towards the European structured invoice: Directive (EU) 2025/516 (ViDA) allows e-invoicing to be required and sets near-real-time information for cross-border B2B transactions from 1 July 2030, with 1 January 2035 as the deadline for national systems.f4
  • The tax administration uses AI under human oversight: the 2025 Tax and Customs Control Plan guidelines announce AI projects across the Tax Agency's areas of action, with AI never the last decision instance. The practice should prepare its data for finer cross-checks.f5
  • The practice's clients are SMEs and the self-employed with low adoption (17% of small EU enterprises; 21.4% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees): they may ask their advisers which tools to use with accounting and tax data.f6f7
  • The duty of confidentiality and the GDPR require knowing which tool each tax and accounting datum goes to; an unreviewed AI answer is never advice. The AI Act adds obligations depending on role and use.f9f8

Asset managers and financial advisers 12 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Adoption is partial and uneven. According to ESMA's 2025 survey, 45% of firms have no AI use case in production or in testing, and 65% of micro firms have no active or planned use cases. Investment firms and asset managers trail other sectors.f2
  • Current use is internal and low-autonomy: 87% of reported use cases are internal only and the most common is drafting and summarising information. Robo-advice and AI-driven portfolio management remain rare and most are still at development or testing stage.f2
  • Supervisors have already said the rules do not change: ESMA expects firms using AI to comply with MiFID II (organisation, conduct of business and the duty to act in the client's best interest), and the CNMV reminds that automated advice requires the same conduct rules and the suitability test.f1f4
  • In asset management, AI helps decide but does not decide: according to ESMA, managers mainly use generative AI to support human-driven investment decisions, and funds that promote their use of AI remain a small part of the industry, without significantly better or worse performance.f3
  • Training and shared standards are missing: 85% of employers surveyed by CFA Institute see a need for industry-wide AI standards and ethical guidelines, 70% need training on AI regulatory compliance and risk, and 47% believe their organisation is not well prepared for regulatory changes.f6
  • Specific risks: automated advice and the duty to act in the client's best interest (MiFID II), dependence on a few technology providers (DORA; 62% of surveyed firms use commercial cloud only) and clients' personal data (GDPR). The AI Act classifies creditworthiness assessment of natural persons as high-risk. Each use case needs a person who reviews or decides.f1f5f2f8f7f9

Insurance brokers 11 use cases · 7 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • The European supervisor already sets expectations that reach intermediaries: EIOPA's opinion of 6 August 2025 is addressed to national authorities and covers the activities of insurers and intermediaries that use AI. It creates no new requirements: it explains how current rules apply, with a risk-based, proportionate approach.f1
  • When the insurer decides with AI, the broker must be able to explain it to the client: the opinion says that, where relevant, insurers should inform intermediaries when a decision is made on the basis of an AI system so that they can meet their legal obligations towards customers.f1
  • The broker's value is advice, and the law defines it: when advice is given, the distributor must provide a personalised recommendation explaining why a specific product best meets the client's needs, and an objective analysis requires comparing a sufficient number of contracts in the market. AI can prepare the analysis; the recommendation belongs to the professional.f2f6
  • Continuing training is mandatory, at least 15 hours a year under Spanish law. The rule does not cover AI, but it is the natural moment for the brokerage to train its team in the responsible use of these tools.f2
  • The sector is small and fragmented: as of 21 November 2025 there were 3,445 insurance brokers and brokerage companies, and individual brokers fell by 8.86% compared with 2024. BIPAR states that intermediaries that are SMEs or microenterprises are exempt from DORA, although some requirements may still apply if the insurer treats them as ICT service providers.f3f4
  • Specific risk: the brokerage processes clients' personal data, sometimes health data, which the GDPR protects more strictly. The AI Act treats risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance as high-risk; the brokerage does not perform that task, but must know what each tool does with the data and always keep a person who reviews.f7f5f1

Estate agencies and property management 12 use cases · 8 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • Estate agents already use AI daily, mostly for writing: according to the 2026 technology report of the US National Association of Realtors (NAR), 23% use it every day and the most common use is writing listing descriptions (75% of those who use it). The data is from the United States, but it shows where the sector starts.f5
  • Automated valuation helps but does not replace the valuer. The European Banking Authority guidelines on loan origination allow a desktop valuation supported by statistical models only for residential property in mature markets, with the valuer remaining responsible and another method if the model signals low robustness. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) argues for a professional human in the loop.f3f4
  • Anti-money-laundering rules reach property brokerage: Law 10/2010 covers those who professionally act as agents or intermediaries in property sales or lettings when the transaction involves rent of at least EUR 120,000 a year or EUR 10,000 a month. The client must be identified with reliable documents before dealing, and records kept for ten years.f1
  • Property management involves repetitive, heavily regulated tasks. In its 2025 magazine the General Council of Property Administrators' Colleges says AI systems promise to transform internal management, especially the most routine tasks. The Horizontal Property Act sets what cannot fail: notice periods, a minute book with signatures and five-year retention of documents.f6f2
  • Specific risk for the sector: deciding who gets access to a home is a decision about people. Ranking enquiries or reviewing a tenant's documents can end in discrimination or in a creditworthiness assessment, which the AI Act treats with particular care. Before using tools with applicants' data: a legal basis (GDPR), clear rules on which data is requested and a person who decides. Images retouched with AI carry a clear notice.f8f7
Figures8 sourced figures
  • 23 % · Agents using AI tools every day (NAR, United States, 2026)f5
  • 75 % · AI users who use it to write listing descriptions (NAR, 2026)f5
  • 55 % · Respondents saying AI has had a positive effect on their business (NAR, 2026)f5
  • 120.000 € / 10.000 € · Annual or monthly rent from which property brokerage is an obliged entity under the anti-money-laundering lawf1
  • 10 años · Years identification and due-diligence records must be kept (Law 10/2010)f1
  • 6 días · Minimum notice for the ordinary annual meeting of the owners' associationf2
  • 5 años · Years the secretary keeps notices, communications and proxiesf2
  • 3 años · Previous calendar years for which a buyer answers for the community's debts, plus the expired part of the year of purchasef2

Restaurants, bars and cafés 11 use cases · 8 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Food waste is now a legal duty: Law 1/2025 requires food-chain operators to apply the hierarchy of priorities (Article 6) and sets for 2030 a 50% reduction in food waste per capita at retail and consumer level and a 20% reduction in losses along production and supply chains.f1
  • Hospitality businesses must make it easy for customers to take away, at no extra cost, what they do not eat (except at all-you-can-eat buffets or similar), say so clearly and visibly on the premises and use food-grade, reusable or easily recyclable containers (Article 8).f1
  • Allergen information is mandatory for non-prepacked food too, such as that served in a restaurant or bar; in Spain it is regulated by Royal Decree 126/2015. An out-of-date menu is a direct risk to the customer.f2
  • HACCP-based procedures are mandatory in all food establishments, with prior good hygiene practices and documents and records proportionate to the nature and size of the business. Records are a daily burden that can be assisted, not replaced.f3
  • The sector has a public digitalisation plan: SEGITTUR and Hostelería de España published the Digital Activation Plan for the tourist HORECA sector in June 2026, and its study concludes that digitalisation does not depend only on the owner's willingness. Among small businesses, 21.4% of Spanish enterprises with fewer than 10 employees use AI.f4f6
  • Specific risk for restaurants and bars: an allergen error can harm a customer, so a responsible person always checks the information before it is published. Bookings and orders also contain personal data (GDPR), and uses that manage people, such as rotas or recruitment, may be high-risk under the AI Act.f2f8f7

Local shops and online stores 12 use cases · 8 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • Selling online is no longer only for the big players: in 2024, 23.59% of EU enterprises and 21.38% of small ones sold online, although e-commerce brings small ones only 8.65% of their turnover. The local shop with an online channel is the normal case, not the exception.f1
  • E-commerce in Spain turnover exceeded EUR 114.8 billion in 2025, up 20.6% on the previous year, according to the CNMC. The figure includes many travel and transport transactions, but it sets the pace: online demand grows and the small shop competes for it.f2
  • Customers already search with AI before buying: 61% of European consumers use AI to discover and evaluate products, and sector analysts expect agent-led shopping to be the biggest structural shift since online commerce, although fully autonomous purchasing remains limited. For a small shop, a well-built product listing becomes its shop window to these assistants.f3
  • Small retailers want to save time and ease staff shortages, but run into tight budgets, limited time and lack of expertise. In a real demand-forecasting case in Germany, staff trusted the tool more over time and gained time for selling. The key is to start with one task and measure it.f4
  • Large retailers still do not focus investment on what matters most in a shop: only 15% direct it to pricing, promotions and assortment, and eight in ten executives say it is too early to measure the impact on profit. Test small, with a baseline figure and without promising savings.f3
  • Specific online-retail risk: EU consumer law requires telling consumers when a price is personalised through automated decision-making, showing the lowest price of the previous thirty days as the prior price in a sale, and not presenting fake reviews; the maximum fine must be able to reach at least 4% of annual turnover. The GDPR and the LOPDGDD also protect customer data in loyalty schemes, and the AI Act requires customers to know when they are dealing with a machine or seeing AI-generated content (Art. 50). A person reviews prices, reviews and sensitive messages.f5f8f6f7
Figures8 sourced figures
  • 23,59 % · EU enterprises with online sales, 2024f1
  • 21,38 % · Small EU enterprises with online sales, 2024f1
  • 8,65 % · Share of small EU enterprises' turnover that comes from e-commerce, 2024f1
  • 114.800 M€ / +20,6 % · E-commerce turnover in Spain in 2025 / change on 2024f2
  • 61 % · European consumers already using AI to discover and evaluate productsf3
  • 15 % · Retailers focusing their AI investment on pricing, promotions and assortmentf3
  • al menos 4 % · Minimum maximum fine required by the consumer modernisation directive, on the trader's annual turnoverf5
  • 30 días · Minimum look-back period for the prior price announced in a sale (lowest price applied)f5
