Local clinics and health services 11 use cases · 11 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • Professional bodies ask for supervised AI: the International Pharmaceutical Federation (policy adopted on 31 August 2025) says pharmacists must always supervise and validate any AI process linked to health care, and the American Dental Association reminds that human expertise and clinical judgement remain essential.f2f5
  • AI is already used to read dental images: the American Dental Association describes algorithms to analyse radiographs and intraoral scans as an aid to diagnosis, and is working on a technical standard to evaluate these systems.f5
  • The US regulator reports more than 1,600 AI-enabled medical devices (September 2026) and says it regulates the device, not AI as such. It is a sign of market maturity, but it is not an authorisation in Europe.f3
  • The European Commission says AI software for medical purposes is high-risk under the AI Act and that AI must fit into the clinical workflow, not be an add-on. Health data can be reused for research and AI training under the European Health Data Space.f4f7f8
  • Specific risk for clinics: health data is a special category under the GDPR and is covered by professional secrecy. Software that advises, diagnoses or prioritises patients may be a medical device with CE marking (Medical Devices Regulation) and high-risk under the AI Act. The Spanish medicines agency answers software qualification queries, non-binding. Before using a tool with patients: legal basis, processor contract, CE marking where applicable and the professional always decides.f10f11f9f7f6
Figures4 sourced figures
  • más de 1.600 · AI-enabled medical devices on the US regulator's page (September 2026)f3
  • 31-08-2025 · Adoption date of the International Pharmaceutical Federation policy on AI in pharmacy practicef2
  • 90 días naturales · Maximum period for the Spanish medicines agency's report on a medical device qualification query, from validation of the requestf6
  • 1-08-2024 · Entry into force of the AI Act, which classes AI software for medical purposes as high-riskf4

Education and training 10 use cases · 8 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • Young people already use AI to study: according to Eurostat data cited by the European Commission, 4 in 10 EU residents aged 16 to 24 used generative AI for formal education in 2025. A centre that does not set rules still has it in the classroom.f3
  • A better task is not better learning: the European Commission reports that students benefit most when AI supports their own thinking, that educational tools generally outperform general-purpose ones and that over-reliance on AI may weaken critical thinking.f3
  • The teacher stays at the centre: UNESCO proposes a human-centred approach with ethical, safe, equitable and meaningful use, and an age limit for independent conversations with generative AI. The Spanish INTEF guide (version 2.0, September 2026) recommends prioritising tools provided or authorised by the education authorities.f1f5
  • Training is lacking: only 29.7% of EU teachers surveyed in TALIS 2024 had received professional development on AI for teaching and learning. The European Commission's ethical guidelines help teachers with little digital experience.f3f2
  • Specific risk for education: minors are involved and student data needs reinforced protection. AI systems that assess learning outcomes, decide access or admission or monitor exams are high-risk under the AI Act, and systems that infer students' emotions are a prohibited practice in education. The Spanish data protection agency and other authorities remind that using an educational platform is not voluntary for students and families, and ask for an impact assessment, a processor contract and data protection by default.f7f8f6f4f5
Figures4 sourced figures
  • 4 de cada 10 · EU residents aged 16 to 24 who used generative AI for formal education, 2025f3
  • 29,7 % · EU teachers surveyed in TALIS 2024 who had received professional development on AI for teaching and learningf3
  • 10 · Basic principles in the data protection authorities' decalogue for contracting and using educational platforms (23 March 2026)f4
  • 2.0 (septiembre de 2026) · Current version of the Spanish Ministry of Education guide on AI in educationf5

Marketing, advertising and communication 12 use cases · 11 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • AI is already a working tool in advertising: according to IAB Europe, 85% of surveyed companies (advertisers, agencies, ad tech and publishers) use AI tools for marketing, and 60% of ad tech firms and 48% of agencies report KPI improvements. A small agency that does not use it competes at a disadvantage.f1
  • Advertisers want clear rules: of 27 large brands, 78% use AI-generated or AI-enhanced content in consumer-facing marketing, 67% have internal rules and eight in ten want global guidance; most think an AI voice that could be mistaken for a person should be disclosed. Clients will expect the agency to say what is AI and what is not.f4
  • Intellectual property is the main worry: 77% of brands in a WFA study point to the IP and copyright risks of generative AI. The EU intellectual property office describes the clash between using works to train models, authors' rights reservation (opt-out) and licensing; the US Copyright Office concludes that, with current technology, prompts alone do not give enough control to be an author and that purely AI-generated material is not protected.f5f2f3
  • Self-regulation is already moving: the influencer-advertising code of conduct of AUTOCONTROL, aea and IAB Spain came into force on 1 October 2025 with specific provisions on AI-generated content. Anyone producing pieces for brands needs to know and apply it.f6
  • Specific sector risk: the AI Act (Art. 50) requires marking synthetic content and deepfakes, and the Commission has published a code of practice on marking and labelling and Art. 50 guidelines. The GDPR and the LOPDGDD also limit segmentation with personal data, and generated output may copy third-party works. A person reviews each piece before publication, and the client contract says who is liable for what.f8f10f9f11f7

Trades, renovations and home services 9 use cases · 9 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • The trades are mostly one-person businesses. In September 2026 there were 3,505,556 self-employed people registered with Social Security; 85.9% have no employees and 12.0% work in construction. For a sole trader, useful AI is the kind that saves hours of paperwork and phone calls, not the kind that requires building a system.f1
  • AI is reaching the smallest firms: 17% of small EU enterprises (10 to 49 employees) and 21.36% of Spanish ones with fewer than 10 employees use AI. The usual starting point is text: quotes, messages to clients and work reports.f6f7
  • Technical paperwork is mandatory and has a named person responsible. The low-voltage electrotechnical regulation requires the installing company to issue the installation certificate and lodge it with the regional authority. The thermal installations regulation requires a maintenance log and an annual certificate where a maintenance contract is mandatory. AI prepares the draft; the qualified professional signs.f2f3
  • A renovation leaves long liabilities. The Building Act sets liability for damage of ten years (structure), three years (habitability) and one year (finishes). Keeping photos, work reports and materials in order for each job is the best defence against a claim.f4
  • Specific risk for the trades: work is done in clients' homes, with their photos, addresses and keys, and sometimes with staff on the move. You need a legal basis, process only the data you need and not keep photos of a home's interior longer than necessary (GDPR). Tracking a vehicle's route is not monitoring a person: AI systems that manage workers are a sensitive use, and the AI Act treats them with particular care.f5f9f8

Workshops and small manufacturers 12 use cases · 10 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • The Data Act already applies: the European Commission says it is applicable from 12 September 2025 and that the user of a connected product, such as a car or industrial machinery, has the right to access the data it generates and share it with third parties, including repair providers. For a workshop, more vehicle and machine data within reach.f1
  • The Commission has published guidance on vehicle data accompanying the Data Act, which also covers aftermarket service providers, and a delegated regulation of 23 March 2026 prevents a manufacturer from making independent operators' access to diagnostic and repair information conditional on requirements other than those of the type-approval regulation, for example for cybersecurity reasons.f2f3
  • The new Machinery Regulation will be fully applicable from 20 January 2027, according to Spain's National Institute for Safety and Health at Work, and its higher-risk categories include safety components with self-evolving behaviour that use machine learning. Anyone who makes or modifies machines, however small, should follow it closely.f4f9
  • Automation is rising in workplaces and brings new opportunities and risks for safety and health, according to the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA), which proposes assessing them task by task.f5
  • Specific risk for workshops and small manufacturers: an AI tool that touches a machine or its safety function changes the machine's risk assessment (Machinery Regulation), photos of customers and vehicles may contain number plates and people (GDPR) and an AI system that is a safety component of a regulated product may be high-risk (AI Act). A responsible person always reviews the diagnosis, the quote and any safety decision.f9f10f8

Small haulage and self-employed carriers 10 use cases · 10 sources
Where it is heading4 trends
  • The transport document is going digital in the European Union: the European Commission says the eFTI Regulation aims to replace paper with electronic data in all transport modes, that it will apply in full on 9 July 2027 and that Member State authorities must accept information shared through certified platforms.f1
  • In Spain, the administrative control document for public road freight transport must be digital ten months after Law 9/2025 of 3 December came into force, and so must the route sheet for passenger transport. A resolution of 5 June 2026 sets out how the software that manages it must work. It applies to domestic transport and cabotage, not to international transport.f3
  • The second-version smart tachograph reaches vans too: the European Commission states that light commercial vehicles over 2.5 tonnes in international transport must have it by 1 July 2026. More driving and rest data, and more control over it.f2
  • Specific risk in transport: tracking drivers with GPS, tachograph or cameras means processing workers' data. The Spanish Data Protection Agency reminds that geolocation of company vehicles rests on the employment contract and not on consent, that the driver must be informed, that minimisation applies and that an in-cab camera recording video and sound to monitor driving does not override the driver's data protection rights. Any AI that monitors fatigue or driving needs an impact assessment, prior information and human review; AI systems for managing people may be high-risk, and platform workers have their own protection.f4f7f10f8f9

Agri-food 12 use cases · 5 sources
Where it is heading5 trends
  • The field notebook is going digital: Order APA/204/2023 sets the content of the digital farm notebook (plant-protection treatments, fertilisation, treated seed) and makes attaching the fertilisation plan mandatory. A tidy digital record is the basis for any help from AI.f4
  • AI adoption in agriculture is uneven and obstacles weigh more on smaller players: limited access to quality data, development costs, lack of interoperability and uncertainty about regulatory compliance, according to the European Commission's July 2025 report.f3
  • The average EU farm is small: about 3 in 5 farms are under 5 hectares. Solutions designed for a large estate do not work unchanged on a small family farm.f1
  • The European Parliament study notes that data-driven tools work best on larger farms with standardised layouts, and that technology will be needed that works without always relying on the cloud or a good connection.f2
  • Specific risk for the sector: who owns the farm's data and who depends on whom. The European Parliament study warns that farmers may end up owning their land but renting their data and digital equipment from large companies. Before signing with a supplier: data ownership, the right to take data away in a readable format and a plan B if the connection fails.f2f5

Associations and non-profits 10 use cases · 8 sources
Where it is heading6 trends
  • AI use is now the majority position among UK charities, though readiness lags: according to the Charity Digital Skills Report 2026, 79% of charities use AI, 56% say lack of skills is their biggest barrier and 33% say their board has poor AI skills.f3
  • Trust is the weak point: 35% of organisations do not trust AI tools, more than double the previous year. For an organisation that lives on the trust of members and donors, its use of AI must be explainable.f3
  • Funders also use and notice AI: 58% say AI is changing the bids they receive and 55% do not know whether applicants use it. AI-written bids will become more common, but quality and accuracy standards do not change.f3
  • Regulators ask for human accountability and transparency: the Charity Commission reminds trustees that they remain responsible for decisions and must not delegate them to AI, and the Fundraising Regulator asks for proportionate human oversight, transparency where content could mislead donors or the public, and recommends having an AI policy.f1f2
  • In Spain the third sector is large and lives on people: in 2024 the Plataforma de ONG de Acción Social grouped 36 organisations with 165,783 employees and 470,438 volunteers. A small organisation can copy good practice, such as the internal AI-use policy published by the Plataforma del Voluntariado de España in 2026, with lists of permitted, supervised and prohibited uses.f4f5
  • Specific risk for the sector: it works with vulnerable people and sensitive data. Health or social-situation data are special categories (GDPR and LOPDGDD), and AI systems that decide access to benefits or essential services are among the high-risk ones in the AI Act. Starting rule: AI helps prepare; any decision about a person is always human, and no personal data is pasted into tools without a contract and a legal basis.f8f6f7f5

Member and donor management and churn preventionPredictive ML01 · CustomerAugment

Flags which members or donors may leave and proposes a thank-you or contact message; the person decides whom to call and how.f2f8

Function
Members and donors
Value lever
Revenue
Technology and usual techniques
Predictive ML. Models that learn from historical data with a known outcome. Most used with tabular data: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM), random forests and logistic regression as an explainable baseline. For anomalies: isolation forests or autoencoders. For time series: statistical models or recurrent networks. Always ask for the comparison with a simple baseline.

AI security: companies and solutions (15 solutions)

A market reading, not a recommendation: companies and solutions that present themselves as an answer to each AI security capability in document 35, with what their own official page says about them, checked on 19-10-2026. SEVEN-G does not assess, endorse or compare products; the list is not exhaustive and is sorted alphabetically. Before using any of them with company data —even to test it— the supplier assessment applies (document 36 and P55).

Runtime guardrails and AI gateways 5 solutions

Control points outside the model that filter inputs, outputs and context, prevent leakage, enforce quotas and log traffic to models.

SEVEN-G security controls: SEG-26, SEG-03, SEG-07, AG-05

CompanySolutionWhat it does (according to its official page)
Amazon Web ServicesAmazon Bedrock Guardrails1Configurable safeguards that detect and filter harmful text and image content, redact sensitive information and detect model hallucinations.
CloudflareAI Gateway2Gives visibility into and control over AI applications: analytics, logging, caching, rate limiting and retries with a fallback model.
Google CloudModel Armor3Screens the prompts and responses of language models to block malicious input, unsafe content and leaks of sensitive data.
MicrosoftAzure AI Content Safety (con Prompt Shields)4Detects harmful user-generated and AI-generated content in text and images; includes Prompt Shields to detect input attacks against a language model.
NVIDIANeMo Guardrails5Openly available Python library for adding safety and policy checks to language model applications, on prompts and replies, without changing the model.

The agentic customer: companies and solutions (23 solutions)

A market reading, not a recommendation: companies, protocols and solutions that present themselves as an answer to one of the four faces of the agentic customer (document 35, section 9.4), with what their own official page says about them, checked on 15-11-2026. Draft protocols are cited as guidance and do not underpin any control. SEVEN-G does not assess, endorse or compare products; the list is not exhaustive and is sorted alphabetically. Before using any of them with company data —even to test it— the supplier assessment applies (document 36 and P55).

Synthetic research and customer simulation 6 solutions

Platforms that simulate customers, audiences or populations with AI to test messages, prices, products or journeys before doing so with real customers. A simulation does not replace real customers.

SEVEN-G controls and sections: P53 §5.3, SEG-27

CompanySolutionWhat it does (according to its official page)

Protocols, detection and identity of agents 4 solutions

Draft protocols and solutions to tell a legitimate agent from a spoofed one and attribute its actions. Draft protocols are cited as guidance: they do not underpin any control.

SEVEN-G controls and sections: SEG-28, AG-01, AG-15, 52 §4.3.6

CompanySolutionWhat it does (according to its official page)
CloudflareWeb Bot Auth1Lets a site confirm that a request comes from an automated bot by checking cryptographic signatures on its HTTP messages, based on a draft protocol; Cloudflare uses it as one of the methods to verify bots and agents.
FingerprintInteligencia de dispositivos y detección de agentes2Identifies returning visitors, including anonymous ones, to stop fraud; for AI agents, it verifies through cryptographic signing and separates legitimate agents from spoofed ones.
IETFWeb Bot Auth (grupo de trabajo, borrador)3Working group standardising how automated clients authenticate cryptographically to websites and share information about their operators. Work in progress: a draft, not a standard.
SierraPersonal Agent Protocol (borrador)4Draft protocol, sponsored by a customer-service agent provider, for personal agents to discover what a company offers and operate with OAuth sessions and read or write permissions. A draft, not a standard.
